props.title: It's Only Talk

sections.content: It's Only Talk represents a pivotal moment in Japanese independent cinema's exploration of mental health and social isolation. Director Ryuichi Hiroki crafts an intimate portrait of a woman dealing with bipolar disorder, following in the footsteps of other powerful Japanese character studies like Tony Takitani (2004) and Bright Future (2003). The film's unflinching look at depression and human connection shares DNA with Nobody Knows (2004), though it takes a more adult-focused approach.

sections.content: Hiroki's signature style, developed in films like Vibrator (2003), shines through in his intimate handheld camerawork and naturalistic performances. The film's protagonist Yuko, played with remarkable subtlety by Shinobu Terajima, recalls the complex female characters in Love Letter (1995) and April Story (1998), but with a more contemporary edge addressing mental health stigmas in Japanese society.

The film's exploration of online relationships and virtual connections predates similar themes in works like Her (2013) and Creative Life (2009), showing how technology can both isolate and connect people struggling with mental health. The way it weaves together multiple character relationships recalls Sway (2006) and The Taste of Tea (2004), though with a sharper focus on psychological realism. sections.content: It's Only Talk sits within a crucial period of Japanese cinema that began addressing mental health more directly, alongside films like Welcome to the Quiet Room (2007) and Memories of Matsuko (2006). This shift marked a departure from the more metaphorical treatment of psychological issues seen in earlier works like Pulse (2001) and Suicide Club (2001).
